Free-text titles or captions typed by kids: a PI and moderation surface. A curated caption list is used instead.
Auto-extending expiry on each view: popular clips would be retained indefinitely, which conflicts with 312.10. Explicit creator renewal with a 90-day maximum is used instead.

OCR text screening of frames: low recall on brief on-screen text and heavy CPU. Structural guarantees (the compositor never rasterizes DOM text, and page text is server-generated) plus reports are stronger and cheaper.
NudeNet: AGPL-3.0. OpenNSFW2 (MIT) is used instead.
Microsoft PhotoDNA or cloud moderation APIs: outside services that would receive kids' frames. Local models plus SHA-256/dHash blocklists plus NCMEC reporting are used instead.

A grown-up gate, or manual pre-moderation of every clip by Jack: contradicts the owner's settled open-sharing decision and kills instant sharing. Automated prescreen with human review only on signals is used instead.

Public galleries, feeds, comments, likes or public view counts: they would turn the site into social media (state minor-social-media laws, OSA duties, AADC nudges). Unlisted link-only is used instead.
robots.txt Disallow for /c/: some unfurlers honour robots.txt and would stop generating previews. noindex via meta tag and X-Robots-Tag is used instead.
twitter:card summary_large_image only: loses Discord's player-style embed. 'player' plus an /embed route is used, and X falls back gracefully.
mp4box.js for validation: a second MP4 library with a callback/append API. mediabunny (already the client muxer) parses moov via range reads in Node (prototyped at 3-62 ms and up to 25 KB read).
Running the screener inside the always-on web process: an OOM or latency problem in ffmpeg/ORT could take the site down. A separate serverless worker isolates it at similar cost.
Letting kids share the link before screening finishes: unfurls are generated at send time, so an early share would freeze a broken preview into recipients' chats.
openQuestions: Which legal entity operates hankshits.com for the DMCA designation? The service provider's street address is published unless the Copyright Office approves a PO box. The same answer feeds the COPPA 'operator' analysis that counsel should confirm.

Admin alert channel for held and reported clips, which runs on the TIDA 48 h clock: use Jack's existing Pushover (already owned, not a new paid service), or the in-app admin dashboard only? The sweeper's 44 h auto-remove backstop keeps TIDA compliance either way.
Retro-arcade: which titles go on the kid-safe hosted allowlist, and does Jack accept 'Retro Arcade' (no ROM title) on public pages?

Railway WRITE grants needed at build time. These are named here, not run: create the hanks-hits-clips bucket in the hanks-hits-storage sidecar; put-bucket-cors; create the clip-screener service (Serverless on) and the clip-sweeper cron service; set the service variables including CLIPS_BUCKET_HOST as a build-time ARG; set a workspace SOFT usage alert; add a Cloudflare cache rule for /c/*.

Guests: the design lets signed-out kids create hosted links with tighter quotas, consistent with 'open sharing for everyone'. Confirm that Jack does not want sign-in required for hosted links. A sign-in requirement would not be a grown-up gate, but it would reduce abuse attribution cost.

verdicts.claim: Railway buckets cost $0.015/GB-month (daily average, rounded up), all S3 API operations are free, and bucket egress through presigned URLs or the S3 API is free. A service uploading to a bucket pays service egress because buckets are not on the private network.

Hobby has a combined 1 TB bucket cap and Pro is unlimited. The hard usage limit suspends bucket reads and uploads and takes workloads offline. The Agent hard limit defaults to $20 on Pro and $5 on Hobby, so the workspace looks like Pro.
verdicts.correction: The Pro inference is sound, because the docs state the $20/$5 Agent defaults. It is still an inference from the limit value, not a plan read.

verdicts.claim: Railway buckets are private and support presigned URLs up to 90 days, copy, tagging and multipart. They do not support lifecycle, versioning, object lock or SSE. Railway docs show createPresignedPost with content-length-range. URLs are virtual-hosted, and each environment has its own bucket.
verdicts.correction: The capability list is right. But Railway's createPresignedPost sample is a generic AWS-SDK snippet. The underlying store (Tigris) documents neither content-length-range nor checksum enforcement for POST (see the next verdict). The docs also say the bucket REGION is chosen once at creation and cannot be changed afterwards. That choice decides whether takedown is immediate (see the Tigris consistency verdict), and the spec never picks it.

verdicts.claim: Tigris supports PutObject with SHA256 checksum, PutBucketCors, presigned GET/PUT/HEAD/DELETE/UploadPart, range GET and multipart. Expiry must be app-driven.
sources: https://www.tigrisdata.com/docs/api/s3/ (tigris-s3.md: presign list is Delete/Get/Head/Put/UploadPart only; PutBucketLifecycleConfiguration is not supported on Railway-style backends)
verdicts.correction: The compatibility matrix does NOT list POST Object. The separate HTML-form doc describes POST policies but never mentions content-length-range. It also says x-amz-* form fields without a matching condition are 'accepted with whatever value the form sends', so the spec's unconditioned x-amz-checksum-sha256 POST field is probably not enforced. What Tigris DOES document: every x-amz-* header on a presigned URL must be signed and must match on use, and PutObject verifies SHA256 checksums. So a presigned PUT with a signed x-amz-checksum-sha256 header binds the exact bytes, which also fixes the size. That is a better-documented path than POST.

verdicts.claim: Hiding a clip with CopyObject c/->q/ then DeleteObject makes every outstanding presigned URL return 404 at once.
sources: https://www.tigrisdata.com/docs/buckets/locations/ (tigris-consistency.md: Global = 'Strong consistency for requests in the same region. Eventual consistency globally', 'Data pulled on demand and cached locally')
verdicts.correction: This holds only for single-region or multi-region Tigris placement. On Global or Dual-region placement, a region that has already cached the object can keep serving it for a while after the DELETE. The spike must create the bucket in one fixed region and test GET-after-DELETE from at least two geographic vantage points, not one.

verdicts.claim: The Cloudflare Service-Specific Terms bar serving video through the CDN on non-Enterprise plans without paid services. A 302 to a presigned bucket URL keeps the bytes off the zone and off service egress (about $1,125/month avoided at 22.5 TB).
Cloudflare edge-caches 302s on .mp4/.jpg for 20 min when no Cache-Control is sent, and 404/410 for 3 min. So explicit max-age and no-store are needed.
verdicts.correction: The TTL facts are right, but the claim misses one behavior. For cacheable extensions, Cloudflare converts HEAD to GET, fills the cache from a GET and returns only the headers. The origin never sees a HEAD for /c/<slug>/v.mp4 or card.jpg, so spec 5.7's 'HEAD returns 302 to a presigned HeadObject' branch is dead code. HEAD clients get the cached GET-signed Location, which S3-style SigV4 rejects when used with HEAD.

verdicts.claim: LinkPresentation (what iMessage uses) follows a 302 for og:image and og:video. It inlines video up to about 10.1 MB and makes larger files tap-to-play.
verdicts.correction: The data is real, but the test called LPMetadataProvider directly on macOS, over plain HTTP, against localhost, with a SAME-ORIGIN redirect and unlimited bandwidth. Production uses a cross-origin HTTPS redirect to *.t3.storageapi.dev and is fetched by the sender's iPhone, often on cellular, inside the 30 s timeout. The about-10 MB threshold matches TN3156, but whether a 9 MB inline preview survives a real phone network is unverified. It stays gated on the real-device test.

verdicts.claim: Discord and Telegram play og:video served as a direct MP4 behind a bare 302, as FxEmbed does.
WhatsApp, Google Messages, Slack, X and Messenger render image cards. The WhatsApp crawl is a sender-device GET, and og:image must be under 600 KB, at least 300 px wide and no wider than 4:1.
verdicts.correction: The cited WhatsApp doc covers Business Platform messages. Consumer-chat previews are built on the sender's device with undocumented rules. The claim is fine as a design input but needs the real-device gate, as the spec already says.

verdicts.claim: The server-side validator prototype accepts mediabunny fast-start output and rejects bad layouts cheaply. The spec's validator 'rejects udta'.
verdicts.correction: The box-walk and moov checks work, but the 'no udta' rule was never implemented. The prototype ACCEPTED a file carrying a handle-plus-game title tag, which is exactly the metadata the spec says it rejects. mediabunny writes udta only when tags exist. However, Conversion copies the INPUT's metadata tags by default, and the spec uses Conversion for long-tier remux. So the client must pass tags: {} explicitly, and the validator must actually implement the rule and have a test for it.

verdicts.claim: The face prescreen is cheap (0.16-0.44 s) and separates real faces (0.91-0.93) from game frames (0.02-0.08). The budget is 2 vCPU-s per clip including NSFW and VAD.
verdicts.correction: Only YuNet was prototyped, on Apple silicon, over 6 game screenshots. OpenNSFW2 (a ResNet-50 variant, far heavier than YuNet) and Silero VAD were never run. The 2 vCPU-s and 0.45 GB figures are extrapolations for Railway's shared x86 vCPUs. The keyframe-only sampling also has a security gap (see the design problems).

verdicts.claim: 16 CFR 312.2 counts 'enabling a child to make PI publicly available' as collection unless PI is deleted before posting AND deleted from records.
FTC COPPA FAQ F.2: the prescreen-and-delete recipe (including geolocation metadata), plus F.3 that blurring faces is acceptable.
The 312.5(c)(7) persistent-identifier exception and the 312.4(d) notice duties apply, and the only pre-existing gap is that signup collects a child's email.
verdicts.correction: The legal reading is correct, but the gap is bigger than stated. The site has NO privacy notice at all today: there is no /privacy route and no 'privacy' string anywhere in src/app. It already collects name, email and password on a child-directed site. The signup copy asks users to 'use a grown-up's email or get permission', which is not COPPA notice.

verdicts.claim: The TAKE IT DOWN Act makes Hank's Hits a covered platform with a 48-hour removal duty, $53,088 per violation.
verdicts.correction: The statute EXCLUDES services that 'consist primarily of content that is not user generated but is preselected by the provider' where interactive functionality is 'incidental to, directly related to, or dependent on' that content. A games site whose clip links depend on its own games plausibly falls in that exclusion. A no-account removal process is still good practice. But calling the 48-hour clock a legal mandate overstates it, and that framing is what justifies the dangerous 44-hour auto-remove-and-blocklist backstop.

verdicts.claim: 18 U.S.C. 2258A preservation is 1 year after the REPORT Act, with NIST-CSF-consistent, limited-access storage.
DMCA agent designation costs $6, lasts 3 years and publishes a street address.
Railway Serverless sleeps 5-10 min after the last outbound packet, and the first woken request may 502. Cron jobs must exit and run at least 5 minutes apart.

Repo constraints: rate-limit.ts is in-memory; reuse getClientIP (x-real-ip, then rightmost XFF); the CSP has media-src 'self' blob: and connect-src 'self' https:; Permissions-Policy lacks display-capture; sw.js has a no-op fetch listener.
verdicts.correction: All confirmed. getClientIP does work behind Cloudflare, because Railway rewrites X-Real-IP from CF-Connecting-IP. It returns the FULL IPv6 address, though. Mobile carriers give each subscriber a /64, so a per-address IPv6 key can be rotated for free. Quota keys must truncate IPv6 to /64 (or /56) before HMACing.

verdicts.claim: The cost model: about $1.50 / $6.55 / $24.50 per month at 1k / 10k / 100k clips, with a worst-case abuse ceiling of about $18 per month.
verdicts.correction: The arithmetic checks out, and the dollar ceiling is real. But the spec's own 100k scenario (1,075 GB) exceeds its 400 GB live_bytes_cap, which auto-pauses hosted links for everyone. The screener line is unmeasured beyond YuNet. The design also optimizes the wrong thing: an always-on screener costs about $4.50/month by the spec's own numbers, which removes the cold-start and 502 machinery entirely.

designSpecProblems: NAME LEAK IN A BUILT-IN GAME: four-wheeler-3d rasterizes kid-typed free text into the WebGL scene. PropertyPanel.tsx:331-336 takes a 10-character outfit.text input, and components/models/OutfitText.tsx:14-26 draws it with fillText into a THREE.CanvasTexture on the rider. The spec's section 10 sets built-in R3F games to hosted 'on'. It rejects OCR because 'the compositor never rasterizes DOM text', but this text is not DOM, it is in the game frame. A kid who types 'SMITH' on a jersey gets a public link showing a surname. That breaks the no-real-names constraint and 312.2. Fix the class, not just this game: (a) the capture registration hook must be able to blank user-typed textures during capture and hosted export (four-wheeler-3d registers an OutfitText override); (b) add a repo test that fails when any store string written from an <input> reaches fillText or CanvasTexture in a game whose hosted policy is not 'off'.

PI CHANNEL IN PAGE TEXT: the score is a client-declared integer up to MAX_CURRENCY (1e12), and section 5.6 prints it in og:title and the page body. A 10-digit phone number fits, e.g. 'Monster Truck: Score 5,551,234,567'. This refutes 'no PI can appear in page text'. Show the score only if it is within a per-game plausible max from the registry AND equals the signed-in player's server-side leaderboard best for that game. Otherwise omit it and let the video HUD speak for itself.

SCREENING IS BYPASSABLE BY CONSTRUCTION: the threat model is the forged upload, but step 6.1 decodes only keyframes ('-skip_frame nokey'). The forger chooses where keyframes go (the validator allows 2.5 s gaps), and P-frames can carry arbitrary intra-coded blocks. So a face or nude content placed between keyframes is never scored. Decode every frame and sample at a fixed rate (2-4 fps via the fps filter, plus scene-change frames). Budget roughly 2-6 vCPU-s per 30 s clip, which is still cents per thousand clips.

dHASH BLOCKLIST POISONING: gameplay frames are low-entropy and repeat across players. DOM-replay renderers (chess, checkers, quoridor, 2048, memory-match) draw pixel-IDENTICAL frames for identical states such as the opening board. One removed chess clip whose keyframes enter clip_dhash_blocklist will HOLD every later chess clip that starts from the initial position (more than 3 matches at Hamming distance 6 or less). Combined with 5.9 (hide on the first unreviewed intimate_tida report) and 8e (auto-remove plus blocklist at 44 h with no human), anyone can poison a whole game with one click. Only add dHashes after a human confirms the removal. Exclude frames that match a per-game corpus of common frames. Never auto-blocklist from the 44 h backstop.

GLOBAL KILL SWITCH IS ATTACKER-CONTROLLED: step 5.1f reserves bytes at GRANT time, before any upload. When the reservation fails it flips clip_settings.mode to the sticky 'uploads_paused'. An attacker spreading long-tier grants (52 MB each) across IPs can fill the 400 GB reservation without uploading a byte, and hosted links stay down for everyone until Jack resets the mode by hand. The hold-rate trip (more than 25% of the last 50 clips) and the screener-error trip (more than 20%) are just as easy to trigger, with about 13 forged face clips or with files that pass the box walk but crash ffmpeg. Track pending_bytes separately with about a 16-minute TTL (the policy expiry). Trip only on committed bytes. Scope trips to the offending IPv6-/64, IP or device cluster. Auto-recover with backoff instead of latching.

IDENTITY KEYS DO NOT HOLD UP: (a) IPv6 is keyed per full address, while carriers hand each subscriber a /64 (RFC 6177), so per-IP caps cost the attacker nothing; truncate to /64 before HMAC. (b) hh_did is an ordinary cookie that the attacker simply drops, so device caps constrain only honest kids. (c) K_day rotates the IP HMAC daily, yet the spec relies on cross-day identity: 5.9 'reporter with more than 10 overturned reports loses auto-hide power', 5.11 'purge by IP-hmac cluster', and 12 'repeat-infringer policy per device'. None of these can work with day-rotated keys. Specify a stable keyed HMAC for reputation and repeat-infringer keys, with its own written retention.

NEXT.JS 16 STREAMS og TAGS INTO <body> FOR UNLISTED USER-AGENTS: node_modules/next/dist/shared/lib/router/utils/html-bots.js (Next 16.2.9) blocks metadata into <head> only for listed bots. Every other UA gets metadata appended to <body> after streaming (Next docs, 'Streaming metadata'). Section 5.6 promises 'og tags identical for every UA' and edge-caches the HTML for 5 minutes without UA in the cache key. So if a human opens the link first, Cloudflare serves the body-metadata variant to later unfurlers. Set htmlLimitedBots: /.*/ in next.config, or render /c/[slug] as a Route Handler that returns hand-built HTML. The Route Handler also avoids deploy-skew chunk 404s from HTML that references old /_next chunks while it sits in the 5-minute cache.

HEAD HANDLING IS DEAD CODE: Cloudflare converts HEAD to GET for cacheable extensions (.mp4, .jpg) and answers HEAD from the cached GET response (developers.cloudflare.com/cache/concepts/cache-behavior). Section 5.7's HEAD -> presigned-HeadObject branch never runs, and HEAD probers receive a GET-signed Location. Either send Cache-Control: no-store on the tiny 302s (2.5M hits x 0.7 KB is about $0.09/month of egress, and it also removes the 5-minute stale-302 takedown window) or drop the HEAD branch and accept the behavior.

UPLOAD BINDING RESTS ON UNDOCUMENTED TIGRIS BEHAVIOR: exact-size enforcement relies on Tigris enforcing ['content-length-range', n, n], which is absent from both the Tigris S3 matrix and its POST doc. The x-amz-checksum-sha256 POST field has no condition, and Tigris documents that unconditioned x-amz-* fields are accepted with any value. The rejected-alternatives entry 'presigned PUT cannot bind size' is wrong. The AWS SDK v3 presigner supports signableHeaders and unhoistableHeaders (smithy RequestPresigningArguments), Tigris requires signed x-amz-* headers to match on presigned URLs, and Tigris verifies PutObject SHA256 checksums. A presigned PUT with a signed x-amz-checksum-sha256 therefore binds the EXACT bytes. Spike both paths. If POST is kept, also add ['eq','$acl','private'] and test that unlisted fields (acl=public-read, Content-Disposition) are rejected.

TAKEDOWN IS NOT IMMEDIATE ON EVERY BUCKET PLACEMENT: Tigris Global and Dual-region buckets are only eventually consistent across regions and cache data per region. The spec never chooses the Railway bucket region, and the region cannot be changed later. Pin a single region at creation, and make verification gate 1 test GET-after-DELETE from two continents.

OWNERSHIP IS LOST ON iPHONE: the delete/renew key lives in client storage. Safari deletes script-written storage for origins with no user interaction in 7 days of browser use, while server-set cookies are exempt (/tmp/hh-clips/fc-webkit-storage.md lines 142, 320). A kid who shares on Monday and returns 8 days later cannot delete or renew the clip. Accept the HttpOnly hh_did cookie (or the signed-in account) as a second owner credential. Keep a 'My Links' list that syncs to the account for signed-in kids.

HOSTED EXPORT IMPLIES AN ON-DEVICE TRANSCODE THE SPEC NEVER BUDGETS: the instant-replay ring holds packets already encoded at a bitrate chosen before the clip length was known. Title and end cards cannot be spliced in without re-encoding either. The kbps formula (about 1.06 Mbps for 60 s) therefore means a full decode and re-encode on the phone or Chromebook. That needs to run with the game paused, in a Worker, with a progress bar. It also needs an overshoot retry loop, because hardware VBR encoders routinely beat a 3% margin (the budget is 9,000,000 x 0.97).

CLIPS DIE IF THE KID SWITCHES APPS: finalize requires the client. A kid who taps 'Get a link' and jumps to Messages gets the page suspended by iOS, so finalize never runs. Section 8b then deletes the pending_upload row after 1 hour even though all 3 objects landed. The sweeper should HEAD the objects on pending rows and finalize server-side. The client should persist the job in IndexedDB and resume it on return.

SERVERLESS SCREENER IS A FALSE ECONOMY: a Node + onnxruntime + ffmpeg + 25 MB model image will cold-start in well over 15 s. On fast Wi-Fi the 9 MB upload takes 2-5 s, so the wake-at-grant trick does not hide the cold start, and the design needs 502 retries plus sweeper re-pings. By the spec's own numbers an always-on screener costs about $4.50/month of RAM. Keep it warm and fold the sweeper into it as an in-process scheduler, which removes a service, a cron and the wake path.

LEGAL HOLD IS NOT LIMITED-ACCESS: lh/ sits in the same bucket as everything else, behind the single full-access key shared by web, screener and sweeper. One sweeper bug or a leaked web env can destroy or read preserved material, which conflicts with 2258A(h)(3) and (h)(5) (NIST-CSF). Use a separate bucket whose credentials exist only in the admin legal-hold action.

ADMIN SURFACE IS TOO WEAK FOR WHAT IT GUARDS: next-auth credentials (password only) plus an allowlist protects a queue that may contain apparent CSAM and legal holds. Add a passkey or TOTP (free, no new service). Write a no-view-beyond-necessary procedure for suspected CSAM that goes straight to report and preserve.

REPORT WEAPONIZATION HAS NO ESCAPE HATCH: one report hides any clip (real_person, private_info or intimate_tida). The admin alert channel is still an open question, so a falsely hidden clip stays dead until it expires, and the owner is never told. Show the owner 'A grown-up is checking this one'. Push admin alerts (for example Pushover, which is already owned). Add an auto-restore rule for reports from low-reputation reporters on clips with clean screener scores.

THE RETRO-ARCADE ALLOWLIST CANNOT BE ENFORCED: the ROM id is client-declared, so any title can be claimed as an allowlisted one. Railway's Acceptable Use Policy (railway.com/legal/acceptable-use) forbids hosting 'copyrighted or pirated ... media ... without proper authorization'. Public clips of commercial ROMs amplify an existing exposure, and enforcement would hit the whole workspace, including the clips bucket and the site. Default retro-arcade to hosted 'off' until ROM licensing is settled.

NEW KID-BUILT GAMES ARE NOT COVERED: '50 real clips per game, re-run whenever a game is added' cannot scale to games kids create over time. generate-game-metadata.ts parses metadata with per-field regexes (lines 28-33), so a nested clips:{...} policy needs a generator change. A missing policy must fail CLOSED ('off'), including for src/apps/* such as drawing-app (freehand names and faces) and weather (a typed town). The put-it-online skill should auto-generate headless calibration clips and require zero holds before it flips a game to 'on'.

SCHOOL NETWORKS ARE AN UNTESTED FAILURE PATH: uploads and playback both hit *.t3.storageapi.dev, an unfamiliar domain that K-12 filters on managed Chromebooks may block. Add a gate on a filtered Chromebook. For a fallback, proxy uploads through the web service on a DNS-only (grey-cloud) subdomain: ingress is free and service-to-bucket egress is about $0.00045 per 9 MB clip. A grey-cloud host keeps the bytes off the Cloudflare CDN, so the SST ban does not apply.

MINOR next.config.ts ISSUE: headers() cannot UNSET X-Frame-Options for /c/:slug/embed, because the global '/:path*' rule also matches and 'last match wins' only overrides values. Either exclude the path with a negative-lookahead source, or rely on CSP3 frame-ancestors overriding XFO in modern browsers, and write down which.

MINOR DEDUPE ISSUES: 5.1d dedupes only against 'live', while the partial unique index also covers screening, held and hidden, so a re-grant during screening hits a unique violation and returns a 500. Dedupe also hands another owner's slug (and handle) to a second uploader of the same bytes, and that uploader then cannot delete or renew it.

MINOR PAGE ISSUE: the cached /c/ HTML embeds 12 h presigned URLs, so a tab left open longer fails to play. Either use the stable /c/<slug>/v.mp4 as the <video> src, which keeps signatures out of cacheable HTML (the 302 is one extra hop), or refresh the src on the video's error event.

10/10 GAPS ON THE RECIPIENT PAGE: no muted autoplay loop with tap-to-unmute; no read-aloud button, although the project requires that important instructions for young kids are never text-only; no kid-friendly relative expiry ('gone in 30 days'); and no second-tap share step after the async 'live' status (navigator.share needs transient activation).
missedIssues: There is no privacy policy or COPPA online notice on the site at all today. There is no /privacy route, and 'privacy' appears nowhere in apps/web/src/app, even though signup collects name, email and password. This is bigger than the 'signup email' gap the track filed. Because it is a pre-existing COPPA gap on a child-directed site, the delivery rules treat it as a fix-now item, not a filed issue.

The four-wheeler-3d outfit text (PropertyPanel.tsx:331, OutfitText.tsx:14-26) means typed text is already rasterized by a built-in game, not only by kid-built games. The 'no OCR' decision rests on a false structural premise.
Next.js 16 streaming metadata puts og tags in <body> for unlisted UAs, and Cloudflare's UA-agnostic HTML cache makes that variance reach unfurlers.
Cloudflare converts HEAD to GET for cacheable extensions, so HEAD handling at the origin is unreachable.
Tigris placement type decides whether takedown is immediate (Global and Dual-region are eventually consistent cross-region), and the Railway bucket region is permanent once chosen.
Tigris documents neither POST content-length-range nor POST checksum enforcement. Presigned PUT with a signed x-amz-checksum-sha256 is the documented exact-bytes binding.
IPv6 /64 truncation for per-IP quotas.
Safari's 7-day eviction of script-written storage destroys the client-held owner key; server-set cookies survive.
Attacker-controllable global auto-trips (reservation, hold-rate, screener-error) turn the cost guard into a denial-of-service switch against hosted links for everyone.
dHash blocklisting is structurally unsafe for deterministic, low-entropy game frames, especially DOM-replay boards.
Keyframe-only screening lets a forger hide content in P-frames.
The score field is an unverified numeric free-text channel (phone numbers) on a public page.

The screener runs ffmpeg on untrusted uploads with no hardening. Use -protocol_whitelist pipe, force -f mp4 with an h264/aac-only decoder allowlist, and run as a non-root user with no outbound network and CPU/memory rlimits per job.
The legal-hold prefix shares the bucket and credentials with routine services, so 'limited access' under 2258A is not met.
Railway's Acceptable Use Policy bars unauthorized copyrighted media, which is workspace-wide exposure for retro-arcade ROMs and their clips.
The admin console for held and reported content has no MFA.
src/apps/* (drawing-app, weather) are not addressed. Hosting must fail closed for any id without an explicit policy.
Kid-built game calibration is not automated, although new games appear continuously.
School web filters on *.t3.storageapi.dev, with no fallback upload or playback path.
The client-side finalize dependency loses clips when iOS suspends the page.
Hosted export needs an on-device transcode that is never budgeted: time, battery, a Worker and the paused-game requirement.
TIDA applicability is doubtful under the 'preselected content' exclusion. Keep the removal form, but do not let a mis-framed 48 h mandate justify unreviewed auto-removal plus blocklisting.
verify.summary:
The cost and serving core holds up against primary sources. Railway bucket egress and S3 operations are free. Storage is $0.015/GB-month. The hard limit is a site-killer. Cloudflare's terms ban video through the CDN, so a 302 to a presigned URL is the right call. FxEmbed shows that Discord and Telegram follow 302s. The 2258A preservation period, the DMCA fee and the COPPA 312.2 and FAQ F.2 readings are all accurate.

Several load-bearing mechanics are wrong or unverified, and the privacy and moderation layer has real holes.

Wrong or unverified mechanics:
1. Tigris's S3 matrix does not list POST Object, and its POST doc never mentions content-length-range. It also says unconditioned x-amz-* fields are accepted with any value, so the exact-size and checksum binding is unproven. Tigris DOES document signed x-amz-* headers on presigned URLs and SHA256-checked PutObject, so a presigned PUT with a signed checksum is the better-documented path. The spec rejected it on a false premise.
2. On Tigris Global placement, reads are only eventually consistent across regions, so 'hide kills every presign at once' depends on a region choice the spec never makes and that cannot be changed later.
3. Next 16.2.9 streams og tags into <body> for user agents outside its bot list, and Cloudflare caches the /c/ HTML without UA in the key.
4. Cloudflare turns HEAD into GET for .mp4 and .jpg, so the HEAD branch is dead code.
5. The validator prototype never implemented the 'reject udta' rule. It accepted a file tagged with a handle and game title, and mediabunny Conversion copies input tags by default.
6. Only YuNet was benchmarked, so the NSFW and VAD cost figures are extrapolations.

Privacy and moderation holes:
1. The built-in four-wheeler-3d game draws kid-typed outfit text into its WebGL scene (OutfitText.tsx). That leaks names into public clips and knocks out the premise behind rejecting OCR.
2. The client-declared score, up to 1e12, is printed on the public page, so a phone number can ride along.
3. Keyframe-only screening can be bypassed by a forger.
4. The dHash blocklist poisons whole games, because DOM-replay frames are identical across players. The unreviewed 44 h TIDA auto-remove path makes that one click away.
5. The global auto-trips (grant-time byte reservation, hold rate, screener errors) latch hosted links off for everyone and can be triggered by an attacker.
6. Per-IP keys ignore IPv6 /64 rotation, and daily-rotated HMACs break the reputation and repeat-infringer rules the spec relies on.
7. The owner key dies with Safari's 7-day storage eviction.
8. Legal-hold material shares the bucket and full-access key with routine services.

Two more gaps:
- The site has no privacy notice at all today, which is bigger than the signup-email gap the track found.
- Railway's Acceptable Use Policy exposes the whole workspace if retro-arcade ROM clips are hosted.

Recommended changes: presigned PUT with a signed checksum; a single-region bucket; htmlLimitedBots: /.*/ or a Route Handler for /c/; no-store on the 302s; full-frame sampling; human-gated dHash blocklisting; scoped, self-healing trips; /64 keying; cookie- or account-backed ownership; a separate legal-hold bucket; an always-on screener (about $4.50/month); server-side finalize; and fail-closed hosting policies with automated calibration for new games.

findings.claim: From Safari 17 (iOS 17), a browser app's origin quota is up to 60% of total disk and the overall quota is 80%. Other WebKit apps get 15% and 20%. A Home Screen web app gets the same quota as the browser. Eviction removes a whole origin, least recently used first. Origins with an active page or in persistent mode are skipped. Safari 17 no longer prompts for more space. estimate() is fully supported from Safari 17.

WebKit source (main, 2026): persist() succeeds only when the origin's registrable domain is in domainsExemptFromWebsiteDataDeletion(). That set is app-bound domains plus managed domains plus the standalone (Home Screen web app) domain. So persist() in a normal Safari tab effectively always returns false, and in a Home Screen web app it returns true. Quota-based and time-based eviction skip origins that are persisted or active. The default time-based eviction check interval is 7*24h.
sources: https://webkit.org/blog/14403/updates-to-storage-policy/ ('grants a request based on heuristics like whether the website is opened as a Home Screen Web App')

findings.topic: Storage: ITP 7-day deletion also covers OPFS
findings.claim: ITP deletes all script-writable storage after 7 days of Safari use with no user interaction on the site. The list is IndexedDB, LocalStorage, SessionStorage, media keys, and Service Worker registrations and cache. WebKit's ITP deletion type list also includes WebsiteDataType::FileSystem, which is OPFS, so OPFS is not a way around the cap. Home Screen web apps are exempt, keep their own days-of-use counter, and have storage isolated from Safari. Clips saved in a Safari tab therefore do not appear in the installed web app.
sources: https://webkit.org/tracking-prevention/ (7-Day Cap; Home Screen Web Application Domain Exempt From ITP)

findings.claim: OPFS is unavailable in Safari Private Browsing windows. Sites can detect a private window from that failure. Private-mode storage is ephemeral in every browser.

MDN BCD, 2026-09: createSyncAccessHandle is in Safari 15.2, Chrome 102, Chrome Android 109, Firefox 111. createWritable (FileSystemWritableFileStream) is only in Safari 26+. FileSystemFileHandle.move is in Safari 15.2, Chrome 102/109, Firefox 111. FileSystemHandle.remove is Chrome-only, so use removeEntry. StorageManager.estimate is in Safari 17. LockManager and BroadcastChannel are in Safari 15.4. One path covers every target: positioned writes through a SyncAccessHandle inside a dedicated worker.
sources: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/76113945 (iOS createSyncAccessHandle UnknownError report, needs a fallback)

findings.topic: Storage: Chromium and Firefox quotas and persistence
findings.claim: Chromium lets an origin store up to 60% of total disk in both best-effort and persistent mode. Chrome grants persist() silently from site engagement, install or bookmark status, and notification permission. Firefox shows the user a permission prompt. Firefox best-effort storage is limited to min(10% of disk, 10 GiB group). Data is also evicted under storage pressure, least recently used first.

A WebKit engineer on bug 268816 says: on most iPhones the WebContent process has an OS-defined limit of about 1.5 GB. The process can exceed it only when the system is not under pressure. iPads are higher, 4 GB+ on 8 GB devices. Typed arrays and wasm are limited to about 2 GB (Gigacage). There is no JS exception before the kill, only a tab reload.

findings.topic: Memory: iOS page-memory growth under sustained per-frame canvas/WebGL work
findings.claim: An open EmulatorJS issue (May 2026; iOS 17/18, Safari 26.5) reports that iPhone Safari jetsams EmulatorJS after 60-90 s of play. Web Inspector's 'page' memory category grows about 14 MB/s, which matches framebuffer size times fps, while the JS and wasm heaps stay flat. This is a user hypothesis that WebKit has not confirmed. It still matters in two ways: retro-arcade on iPhone may already be unstable, and any per-frame compositor work must be soak-tested on a real iPhone.

MDN BCD, 2026-09: navigator.deviceMemory is Chrome-only. Since Chrome 147 the buckets are 1/2/4/8 on Android and 2/4/8/16/32 on desktop. Safari clamps hardwareConcurrency to 4 or 8. getBattery is Chrome-only, and Firefox removed it. PressureObserver (Compute Pressure) is Chrome 125 on desktop only, not Android. Long Animation Frames timing is Chrome 123+ only. Safari 26 freezes the iOS version in the UA at 18_6, but the Version/26 token still increments.
iOS 26 and iOS 27 support iPhone 11 / SE 2 and later (A13). iPhone XS/XR stop at iOS 18. So a Safari Version/26+ token implies A13 or newer, while Version/16.4-18.x can mean an A11 or A12 phone.

findings.topic: Timing: rAF throttling and refresh rates
findings.claim: iOS Low Power Mode throttles requestAnimationFrame to 30 fps (WebKit bug 168837). Safari throttles cross-origin iframes until the user taps, but both game iframes are same-origin, so they are not affected. By default Safari renders near 60 fps even on ProMotion displays; 120 Hz needs the 'Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps' flag turned off. Chrome runs rAF at the display rate (the spike saw 113 fps on a 120 Hz Mac). Firefox's resistFingerprinting coarsens timers to 100 ms.

AudioContext.state 'interrupted' is supported in Safari 9+ and Chrome 136+. Triggers include calls, other audio apps, and backgrounding. resume() must be called on 'interrupted' as well as on 'suspended'. getOutputTimestamp() (Safari 14.1, Chrome 57, Firefox 70) maps context time to performance.now time for A/V alignment.

Safari does not fire visibilitychange when navigating away, so pagehide must also be handled. freeze/resume events exist only in Chrome. iOS Safari lost WebGL contexts after backgrounding (iOS 16.7-17.x, WebKit 261331), and reports continued into 17.5, so the recorder must survive webglcontextlost on the source canvas.

WebCodecs spec section 11: a codec counts as active only if it produced output in the last 10 s. A UA MAY reclaim any codec that is inactive (even in the foreground) or in the background, by closing it with QuotaExceededError. It MUST NOT reclaim an active background encoder. Chromium engineers say only hardware codecs get reclaimed, and in practice only when too many are allocated. Chrome users do see QuotaExceeded reclamation in background tabs.

WebKit exposes VideoEncoder, AudioEncoder and VideoFrame to Window and DedicatedWorker, and VideoFrame is serializable (SerializedScriptValue handles it). A main-thread VideoFrame can therefore be transferred to an encoder worker on Safari 16.4+.

Measured on Chrome 153, macOS on M5, fresh profiles, both headless and headed. In 7 of 7 fresh browser launches, the first hardware (or no-preference) H.264 VideoEncoder took 7.5-32 s to emit its first chunk. During that time encodeQueueSize sat at 3 and 163-223 frames were dropped. Every later encoder in the same browser process gave first output in 24-32 ms, on other pages, tabs and sizes too. A throwaway 64x64 one-frame warm-up encode on page A removed the stall for a 1280x720 encoder after navigating to page B. prefer-software had no stall. Main-thread fps was unaffected. The effect is not yet measured on Android, ChromeOS or iOS.

Test setup: a 1920x1080 or 2400x1080 WebGL2 source (preserveDrawingBuffer false) with game logic that scales with CPU. The capture path was drawImage into a 1280x720 or 848x480 compositor, then new VideoFrame, then transfer to a worker VideoEncoder (realtime, H.264). Main-thread cost p50/p95: 0.1/0.2 ms at 1x, 0.5/1.0 ms at 4x CPU throttle, 0.6-1.1/1.4-1.9 ms at 6x. Three variants performed the same: DOM compositor, OffscreenCanvas compositor, and createImageBitmap(resizeWidth/Height) posted to the worker. createImageBitmap on the WebGL canvas in the same task gave non-blank frames (luma 208-221). Game fps with and without capture was identical at 1-2x (60.2). When CPU-bound, the drop was 1-8%: 52.4 to 50.0-51.8 at 4x, and 33.8-35 to 32.2-34 at 6x. Hardware encode latency p95 was 12-17 ms. A 2.5 Mbps realtime target produced about 2.3 Mbps (hardware) or 2.5 Mbps (software). These are desktop numbers, not phone numbers.

Recording the raw DPR canvas tanked Monster Truck to 3.6-6.4 fps. A downscaled compositor at 640-960 px wide kept 33.5-34.1 fps (idle 40-42). A WebGL canvas must be read in the same task as the render (R3F addAfterEffect). Chromium web share is limited to 50 MB total and needs the exact MIME type 'video/mp4' with an .mp4 file name.

mediabunny 1.60.0 MP4 fastStart accepts false, 'in-memory', 'reserve' and 'fragmented'. 'reserve' writes a fast-start file with little memory but needs maximumPacketCount on every track. 'fragmented' is append-only and has onMoof/onMdat callbacks that give byte positions. StreamTarget takes position-addressed chunks (compatible with FileSystemWritableFileStream) and has a chunked mode (default 16 MiB, configurable). Packet buffering means tracks should be fed interleaved. There is no special handling for a truncated tail. @mediabunny/aac-encoder (libavcodec WASM) can fill in where AudioEncoder is missing (Safari < 26).

signOutAndClear clears only the registered localStorage keys and broadcasts a reload to other tabs (apps/web/src/lib/auth-client.ts:36-52, apps/web/src/lib/storage-keys.ts:65-94). It never touches IndexedDB or OPFS. Keys ending in -storage, -progress, -save or -game-state are wiped at sign-out, so device-level clip policy keys must avoid those suffixes. credentials signIn uses redirect:false, so the account can change without a page reload, and an in-memory replay ring would then survive into the next kid's session unless it is purged.

public/sw.js has a no-op fetch handler, so nothing intercepts blob URLs. The manifest uses display standalone and orientation landscape (apps/web/src/app/manifest.ts). IOSInstallPrompt shows only on iPhone in non-standalone mode and can be dismissed with localStorage 'ios-install-prompt-dismissed'. It hides while a start card shows (useStartOverlayShowing) and is currently mounted from FullscreenButton, asteroids and cookie-clicker. useGameShell pauses on visibilitychange only when canPause is true (useGameShell.ts:57-69), so the recorder must listen to visibility itself for the 11 canPause={false} games.

The HTML spec passes rAF callbacks a timestamp relative to that document's own timeOrigin. Timestamps from inside the four-wheeler-adventure (srcdoc) and retro-arcade iframes must be shifted by (iframeWindow.performance.timeOrigin - window.performance.timeOrigin) before they share a timeline with the parent's audio anchors. This comes from reading the spec and has not been tested in Safari.

research.designSpec:
TRACK: on-device clip library, memory, performance, lifecycle, timing. All numbers are defaults, and every constant lives in apps/web/src/shared/clips/config.ts. UI copy below is kid-facing and has no em-dashes. Every sheet or toast gets a ReadAloudButton.

0. VERDICT ON THE DRAFT (what changes)
The draft direction is right: WebCodecs, a GOP ring, a PCM ring, and mediabunny muxing at clip time. It is not airtight yet. These are the required changes:
(a) Hardware encoder cold start. The first hardware H.264 encoder in a Chrome process took 7.5-32 s to emit output (measured, 7/7 launches). Add a site-level idle pre-warm, a WARMING state, and a watchdog with a software bridge.
(b) Close idle encoders ourselves after 8 s. WebCodecs may reclaim inactive codecs (no output for 10 s), even in the foreground, with QuotaExceededError, so that error also triggers auto re-create.
(c) Re-creating an encoder can change the avcC. Tag every GOP with a configKey and have the clip assembler respect segments.
(d) Fix output dimensions per game session and letterbox on rotation. Never reconfigure mid-session.
(e) Use a compositor OffscreenCanvas that is never in the DOM (no extra composited layer on iOS). A DOM canvas is used only for the MediaRecorder/captureStream fallback, which WebKit needs attached (bug 240380).
(f) Store the PCM ring as Int16, not Float32 (11.5 MB versus 23 MB per 60 s stereo 48 kHz).
(g) Library bytes go in OPFS through SyncAccessHandle in a worker, which works on Safari 15.2+. createWritable exists only in Safari 26+. Metadata and thumbnails go in IndexedDB.
(h) Safari grants persist() only to Home Screen web apps, and ITP's 7-day deletion includes OPFS. Design the risk UX around that.
(i) Budget Record mode to 46 MB because of Chromium's 50 MB share cap.
(j) Convert iframe rAF times with the timeOrigin offset.
(k) Purge the in-memory ring whenever the session user changes (credentials sign-in happens without a reload).
(l) Add a crash-loop breaker that uses an unclean-exit marker.
(m) Default replay OFF for retro-arcade on iPhone until a soak test passes (EmulatorJS #1220 jetsam report).

1. TOPOLOGY (where the work runs)
Main thread, one ClipService singleton per tab. It lives in a module outside React, so client route changes do not kill it. It contains:
- FrameMeter: rAF deltas plus display-Hz detection.
- CaptureClock.
- Source adapters: 2D canvas, R3F addAfterEffect, iframe, DOM-replay.
- Compositor: OffscreenCanvas 2D. It does drawImage of the game, then drawImage of a cached HUD strip that is redrawn only when HUD values change, then branding.
- Governor.
- Lifecycle wiring.
- A zustand UI store with {state, level, ringSeconds, jobs}.
Worker 'clips-engine' (module worker, worker-src 'self' is allowed):
- EncoderManager
- VideoRing and AudioRing
- ClipAssembler (mediabunny)
- RecordSession
- LibraryIO (OPFS SyncAccessHandle)
- Recovery
Audio: an AudioWorkletNode 'clip-tap' on the shared game-audio bus gets a MessagePort that was transferred to the worker. PCM never touches the main thread. The worklet converts Float32 to Int16 interleaved and posts 2048-frame blocks with {startFrame} (about 23 msgs/s at 48 kHz).
Per captured frame on the main thread:
  onGameFrame(tFrame, src){ meter.frame(tFrame); if(!capturing||!clock.shouldCapture(tFrame, meter.frameInterval)) return; if(inFlight>=2){stats.dropped++;return;} const c0=performance.now(); try{ comp.draw(src); const vf=new VideoFrame(comp.canvas,{timestamp:clock.ts(tFrame),duration:clock.intervalUs}); engine.postMessage({t:'f',vf},[vf]); inFlight++; }catch(e){ lifecycle.sourceError(e); } stats.capCost.push(performance.now()-c0); }
The worker acks every frame after encode(), which drives inFlight.
Measured main-thread cost of this path: p95 0.2 ms at 1x and 1.0-1.9 ms at 4-6x CPU throttle. Encoding runs off-thread. createImageBitmap(src,{resizeWidth,resizeHeight}) with the VideoFrame built in the worker costs the same. Keep it as an alternate path that the calibration can pick if it measures cheaper on a device.
Encoder config: codec probe order avc1.64001f, then avc1.4d001f, then avc1.42e01f (level 3.1, enough for 720p30); latencyMode 'realtime'; bitrateMode 'variable'; framerate 30; avc {format:'avc'}; hardwareAcceleration 'no-preference'. Force a keyframe when ts - lastKeyTs >= 1,000,000 us, and on the first frame after any create. Drop a frame (and count it for the governor) when encodeQueueSize >= 2. Never hold raw VideoFrames: close each one right after encode().

2. DEVICE TIERS (initial choice, then learned)
Output dimensions are 16-aligned, landscape w x h (swap for portrait):
- T3: 1280x720, 30 fps, 3.0 Mbps, ring 60 s, video ring cap 28 MB.
- T2: 1024x576, 30 fps, 2.2 Mbps, ring 60 s, cap 20 MB.
- T1: 848x480, 30 fps, 1.4 Mbps, ring 30 s, cap 7 MB.
- T0: 640x352, 24 fps, 1.0 Mbps, no ring (manual Record only, max 60 s).
Never upscale beyond the source backing size, except pixel-art sources, which upscale nearest-neighbour up to 2x.
Game weight comes from each game's metadata.ts as plain literals: clipProfile {weight:'light'|'heavy', orientation:'landscape'|'portrait'|'auto', replayDefault?:'on'|'off', maxTier?}. Heavy = monster-truck, four-wheeler-3d, four-wheeler-adventure, retro-arcade.
Decision table (first matching row wins):
- No VideoEncoder: T0 through MediaRecorder with a DOM compositor.
- iPhone with Safari Version token < 16.4: T0.
- iPhone with Version 16.4-25.x: light T1, heavy T0.
- iPhone with Version >= 26 (A13 or newer): light T2, heavy T1.
- iPad with Version >= 26: light T3, heavy T2. Otherwise iPad: T1.
- Android Chrome, deviceMemory >= 8 and hardwareConcurrency >= 8 and hardware avc supported: light T3, heavy T2.
- Android, deviceMemory 4: light T2, heavy T1.
- Android, deviceMemory <= 2: light T1, heavy T0.
- Android with no hardware H.264 (isConfigSupported with prefer-hardware returns false): cap at T1, and T0 when deviceMemory <= 4.
- ChromeOS: deviceMemory >= 8 and hardwareConcurrency >= 8 gives T3; deviceMemory 4 gives T2 with a hardware encoder, otherwise T1; less than that gives T1.
- Desktop: deviceMemory >= 8 gives T3, 4 gives T2, otherwise T1.
Calibration runs in WARMING and doubles as encoder warm-up. It encodes 15 frames at tier dimensions. An encoder error moves to the next codec, then to software, then down a tier. A steady-state encode latency p95 > 100 ms or a capture cost p95 > 3 ms drops one tier.
Learning is stored in localStorage key 'hanks-hits-clips-device', which has no cleared suffix, so it survives sign-out. Per device and game it stores {lastStableLevel, stableSessions, uncleanExits[], baseline{hz,fps50,p95,at}, coldStartMs}. A game is promoted one tier after 3 sessions of at least 3 min each with zero step-downs and zero unclean exits. iPhone is capped at T2. Demotion comes from the governor or the breaker.

3. MEMORY BUDGET (steady, incremental to the game)
Video ring = ringS x bitrate. Audio = ringS x 192,000 B/s (Int16 stereo 48 kHz).
- T3: 22.5 MB video (cap 28) + 11.5 audio + 3.7 compositor + <=7.4 in-flight frames + encoder internals (estimate <=20) + worker heap about 5 = about 75 MB.
- T2: about 59 MB.
- T1: about 33 MB.
- T0 Record: about 20 MB.
Against the about 1.5 GB iPhone WebContent limit, iPhone heavy games run T1 (about 2%). A clip job holds references to ring GOPs and does not copy them. It adds <5 MB: AAC encoder plus a 1 MiB StreamTarget chunk. Record mode RAM does not grow with length because fragments stream to OPFS.
Ring eviction: drop the oldest GOP while (newestEnd - secondOldestGOP.start) >= ringS, or while video bytes > cap. Audio evicts on the same time boundary.
Hard rules:
- Never concatenate the ring into one Blob.
- Never keep decoded frames.
- Revoke every object URL when its card unmounts.

4. PERFORMANCE GOVERNOR (the guarantee)
Guarantee: sustained game fps stays >= 90% of the pre-recording baseline. A drop worse than 25% pauses capture within <=3 s. A 10-25% drop is removed within <=16 s by stepping down the ladder. Capture never adds load to a device that is already struggling without it.
Baseline, in priority order:
(1) The persisted per-device/game baseline, if it is less than 14 days old and was taken at the same display Hz.
(2) The first 2 s of active play with capture OFF. Active play means the start overlay is gone, the game is not paused, and the page is visible. Buffering starts after that 2 s.
Refresh the baseline from samples taken while capture is RESTING, using an EWMA with alpha 0.3.
Signals, evaluated every 1 s over a 2 s window with at least 30 samples:
- V1: fps < 0.90 x baseline.fps.
- V2: the share of intervals > 1.5 x display interval I is more than 5 points above the baseline share.
- V3: capture cost p95 > 0.20 x I (3.3 ms at 60 Hz, 1.7 ms at 120 Hz). In Chrome, Long Animation Frames attribution to the capture function adds evidence.
- V4: queue >= 2 on >20% of captures, or encode latency p95 > 3 x captureInterval, or drops > 5%.
- SEVERE: fps < 0.75 x baseline, or encode latency > 500 ms. Go to RESTING immediately.
Ladder:
- L0: 30 fps at tier dims.
- L1: 24 fps where Hz divides by 24 (120/144/48), otherwise 20 fps.
- L2: 15 fps.
- L3: one resolution rung down. This creates a new encoder segment.
- L4: RESTING.
Step down after 2 consecutive violating windows, then wait a 3 s cooldown and evaluate a fresh window. Step up one fps level after 30 s clean with headroom: fps >= 0.97 baseline, capture cost p95 < 0.1 x I, encode latency p95 < 2 x interval. After a capture-attributed step-down, wait 60 s instead. Allow at most 2 step-ups per session, and never raise resolution mid-session.
RESTING probes use backoff 20, 40, 80, 160, then 300 s max. A probe measures fps with capture off. If fps_off >= 0.95 baseline, run a 6 s trial at L2. If fps_off < 0.90, the device is throttled by something else (thermal or background load): stay resting and do not add load.
Suppress stepping while a clip job finalizes plus 2 s. During that time the job yields between packets whenever V1 fires.
Extra gates:
- Chrome getBattery with level < 0.20 and not charging: go to RESTING with the battery reason.
- PressureObserver 'serious' steps down one level. 'critical' goes to RESTING.
- iOS Low Power Mode is inferred when the steady rAF is 30 Hz on a device whose stored max Hz is >= 60. In that case use eco: T1 dims, 30 fps at stride 1.
Always-on replay defaults to OFF (the button becomes manual 'Record') when any of these hold:
- tier T0;
- T1 and a heavy game;
- retro-arcade on iPhone until the soak test passes;
- the metadata says replayDefault:'off';
- the crash breaker has tripped;
- battery < 20% and discharging at session start.
DOM-replay games are always ON because they have zero live capture cost.
Crash-loop breaker: localStorage 'hanks-hits-clips-live' = {sid, gameId, capturing, visible, t} is written on every state change (never per frame). On load, a record with capturing:true and visible:true means an unclean exit while capturing. The first one starts that game one tier lower next session and turns off auto-highlight post-roll. Two in 7 days turn replay OFF for that game. Three device-wide in 7 days turn replay OFF everywhere. Five clean sessions reset the counters. document.wasDiscarded (Chrome) does not count.

5. TIMING
Display Hz is the median rAF delta over 60 frames, snapped to {30, 48, 50, 60, 72, 75, 90, 100, 120, 144, 165, 240} within 5%, and re-checked every 5 s.
Frame time: always use the rAF timestamp, or the timestamp R3F passes to addAfterEffect. Never use performance.now() inside the callback, which only measures cost. Iframe sources add (iframe.contentWindow.performance.timeOrigin - performance.timeOrigin).
CaptureClock:
  shouldCapture(t, fi){ if(isNaN(t0)){t0=t; nextDue=t;} if(t < nextDue - fi/2) return false; nextDue = Math.max(nextDue + interval, t + interval/2); return true; }
  ts(t){ const us=Math.round((t - t0 - pausedTotal)*1000); return last = Math.max(us, last + 1000); }
  resume(t){ pausedTotal += (t - tLastCaptured) - interval; nextDue = t; }
The clock produces an average of about 30 fps at any source cadence (60/90/120/144 Hz, or a 41 fps game) with no drift and no catch-up bursts after a stall. Output is VFR: timestamps are real, so a 200 ms game hitch holds the last frame for 200 ms, exactly as the kid saw it. At 60 Hz and 120 Hz the cadence comes out exactly regular.
If timer granularity is >= 5 ms (Firefox resistFingerprinting), switch to timestamps from frame count x the measured Hz.
Audio mapping: the main thread sends anchors {ctxTime, perfTime} from ctx.getOutputTimestamp() every 2 s and on every resume. The worker computes perf = perfTime + (sampleCtxTime - ctxTime) x 1000 and puts it on the capture timeline with the same t0 and pausedTotal. Add +1 frame of video-lead compensation. The worst case of about 33 ms stays inside the BT.1359 detectability window. Whenever the AudioContext is suspended or interrupted while capture runs, fill the gap with zero samples so A/V never slips. Include an audio track only if the bus ran during the clip window.

6. RECORDER LIFECYCLE STATE MACHINE
Two orthogonal regions: Recorder and Jobs. Jobs are clip, auto-highlight, record-finalize and recovery; they run in a FIFO in the worker and do not block capture.
Recorder states and what the kid sees:
- UNSUPPORTED: button hidden.
- IDLE: not in a game.
- WARMING: the button shows a thin progress ring. A tap says 'Replay is warming up. Try again in a few seconds! ⏳'.
- BUFFERING(level): 🎬 'Clip it!' with an arc showing seconds available.
- RECORDING(level): red dot plus mm:ss and a stop button. It also feeds the ring.
- RESTING: 🎬 with 💤. The first time, a toast says 'Replay is resting so your game stays fast. 💤'. Clip it still works on the ring it already has.
- SUSPENDED: nothing visible. The pause menu says 'Replay paused'.
- SOURCE_LOST: nothing for 5 s, then 'Replay is waiting for the game'.
- RECOVERING: nothing for 3 s, then the same look as WARMING.
- DISABLED_SESSION: the button becomes 'Record' if T0 works, otherwise it is hidden.
Transitions:
- Site idle (any page, requestIdleCallback with a 3 s timeout) and no warm this session: pre-warm with a 64x64 hardware encode of 1 frame, flush with a 60 s timeout, close, and store coldStartMs. This removed the stall for later pages in the measurements.
- surfaceRegistered: IDLE to WARMING. Create the real encoder, calibrate, and sample the baseline if needed. Then go to BUFFERING if replay is ON, otherwise to ARMED-manual.
- Watchdog: no output 2.5 s after the first encode. If the pre-warm is still pending, stay WARMING and drop frames. On desktop-class devices (hardwareConcurrency >= 8, not mobile), bridge at once with prefer-software at the same dims for the rest of the session. On mobile, wait up to 30 s, then use software at T1 if supported, otherwise T0.
- visibilitychange:hidden or pagehide: any active state goes to SUSPENDED. Stop capture. Record mode flushes the current fragment, fsyncs and updates the journal. Mark capturing:false in the live marker. After 8 s idle, flush() and close() the encoder. The ring stays in worker memory.
- visible: SUSPENDED to the prior state. Create an encoder with a first keyframe, call clock.resume, and resume() the AudioContext on the next user gesture if it is 'interrupted' or 'suspended'.
- GameShell pause, start overlay showing again, or canPause=false games during pause screens: go to SUSPENDED-visible. The same 8 s encoder close applies.
- pagehide with persisted=true (bfcache): same as hidden. pageshow with persisted=true: re-create everything. A Record session is finalized on pagehide.
- freeze (Chrome): same as hidden.
- surfaceUnregistered: SOURCE_LOST with a 1500 ms grace. This covers restarts, key remounts and canvas swaps. Re-register within the grace keeps the same timeline. Otherwise treat it as leaving the game. Record mode finalizes and saves (toast on the next page: 'Recording saved! 🎬'). The ring is kept for 5 min as a 'Save my last run' card in My Clips, then dropped.
- webglcontextlost on the source: SOURCE_LOST until webglcontextrestored.
- A VideoFrame construction exception: SOURCE_LOST for that frame.
- Encoder error callback: RECOVERING. QuotaExceededError (reclaimed) re-creates on the next visible frame. EncodingError or OperationError steps down a ladder: same config, then prefer-software, then one tier down, then DISABLED_SESSION. That is 4 failures in 60 s.
- resize, orientationchange or fullscreenchange: output dims do not change. The compositor recomputes a fit-contain rect every frame and letterboxes with brand-colour bars. New dims apply only at the next session.
- session user id change or the sign-out broadcast: purge. Abort jobs, free the rings, close the encoder, revoke object URLs, and go to IDLE.
- clipRequest(15/30/60 s): the worker waits up to 150 ms for outputs of frames with ts <= request (it does not call flush). It then takes the latest configKey segment and starts at the last keyframe <= windowStart, so the clip may start up to 1 s earlier than asked. It enqueues the job. Auto-highlight adds a 3 s post-roll and is limited to one per 45 s and 6 per session.
Error ladder for storage writes: OPFS, then IndexedDB Blob (clips <= 30 s), then an in-memory unsaved clip with a sticky sheet: 'This clip can't stay on this device. Share it or save it to Photos now! 📸'.

7. RECORD MODE AND CRASH RECOVERY
Output: Mp4OutputFormat({fastStart:'fragmented', minimumFragmentDuration:1}). StreamTarget({chunked:true, chunkSize:1 MiB}) writes into a WritableStream that wraps handle.write(data,{at:position}) on a SyncAccessHandle for rec/<id>.fmp4.
onMdat(data, pos) sets journal.lastGoodEnd = pos + data.byteLength. The journal is a fixed 64-byte record in rec/<id>.journal: {lastGoodEnd, lastTsUs, videoCount, audioCount, ownerKey, gameId, t}. Rewrite it in place and flush() the handle every 2 s and on hidden.
Audio: AudioSampleSource, AAC 128 kbps, fed live from the PCM tap. Safari < 26 has no AudioEncoder: lazy-load @mediabunny/aac-encoder, or record without audio if that fails.
Hold navigator.locks 'hh-rec-<id>' for the whole session.
Caps: 180 s or 46 MB. Video bitrate in Record mode is min(tier, 1.9 Mbps), so 180 s x 2.03 Mbps is about 45.6 MB, under Chromium's 50 MB share limit. At 165 s show '15 seconds left! ⏱️'. At the cap, finalize with 'Recording saved! 🎬'. Hidden for more than 10 min also finalizes.
Finalize: stream-remux fMP4 into a fast-start MP4 (fastStart 'reserve' with maximumPacketCount taken from the parsed input, a packet copy, no re-encode), verify it, move it into the library, and delete the .fmp4.
Recovery runs 3 s after any page load, at idle. For each rec/*.journal whose lock is free (navigator.locks.request(name,{ifAvailable:true})):
1. Truncate to lastGoodEnd.
2. Parse with mediabunny Input(BlobSource(file)).
3. If the duration is >= 1 s, remux into the library as kind 'record' with rescued:true, and show 'We saved your recording from last time! 🛟'.
4. Otherwise delete it if it is older than 24 h.

8. ON-DEVICE LIBRARY
Media bytes go in OPFS; everything else goes in IndexedDB.
OPFS layout: /hh-clips/v1/{lib/<ownerKey>/<clipId>.mp4, tmp/<jobId>.part, rec/<id>.fmp4, rec/<id>.journal}.
IndexedDB database 'hh-clips' v1:
- Store 'clips' {id, ownerKey, gameId, kind:'clip'|'auto'|'record', createdAt, durationMs, bytes, w, h, fps, hasAudio, handle|null, kept, sharedAt|null, expiresAt|null, storage:'opfs'|'idb', blob?, thumb (JPEG 320 px about 15 KB from convertToBlob at clip time), rescued?, hostedSlug?}.
- Indexes: [ownerKey, createdAt] and expiresAt.
Why OPFS: getFile() returns a disk-backed File, so previews, shares and uploads never copy bytes into RAM. Positioned writes let mediabunny's 'reserve' fast-start stream straight to disk. It works on Safari 15.2+, Chrome 102/109 and Firefox 111. IndexedDB-only storage would need the whole file in memory first (BufferTarget), about a 2x size RAM spike, and it faces the same eviction rules.
Write protocol:
1. estimate(): need (quota - usage) > 1.5 x expected bytes + 50 MB.
2. mux to tmp/<job>.part, then flush and close.
3. verify: size > 0, Input parses, duration within +/-0.2 s of expected, first video packet is a key frame.
4. handle.move(lib dir, <id>.mp4).
5. Write the IndexedDB row inside navigator.locks 'hh-clips-lib'.
6. BroadcastChannel 'hh-clips' sends {added:id}.
7. The UI says 'Clip saved! 🎬'.
If step 2-4 fails, retry once, then use the IndexedDB fallback, then the unsaved-clip sheet.
Startup reconcile runs under the lock:
- A file with no row is re-indexed by parsing. Never delete a parsable MP4.
- A row with no file means it was evicted: remove the row and count it for the eviction notice.
- tmp files older than 1 h are deleted.
Caps:
- Device library bytes <= min(2 GiB, 0.25 x estimate.quota). Use 1 GiB when estimate is missing.
- Auto clips: <= 20 per owner, 7-day TTL unless the kid taps ⭐ Keep.
- When over the cap: evict expired autos first, then the oldest un-kept autos (any owner). Never auto-delete explicit or kept clips.
- If still over the cap, or on QuotaExceededError, show 'Your clip shelf is full! Pick some clips to delete or save to Photos. 📦' with the biggest and oldest clips and Delete, Share and Save to Photos actions. The new clip waits in memory until this is resolved.
Share: resolve File objects when a card or sheet becomes visible (await fileHandle.getFile()). The Share tap then calls navigator.share({files:[new File([f],'hanks-hits-clip.mp4',{type:'video/mp4'})]}) synchronously inside the gesture. Firefox, and anything else without file share, gets a Download (a[download]).
Owner partitions:
- ownerKey = 'guest' or 'u_' + the first 20 hex characters of SHA-256('hh-clips:v1:' + session.user.id).
- Lists show only the current owner's clips.
- Sign-out hides clips and never deletes them. The grown-up sign-out confirm offers an unchecked option 'Also remove this player's clips from this device'.
- After sign-in, if guest clips exist: 'Move your 3 guest clips to your shelf?'
- Clips hold only game pixels plus the pseudonymous handle, so hiding them (without encryption) is enough.
- Multi-tab: only the visible tab captures. Library writes are serialized by Web Locks. Other tabs refresh on BroadcastChannel messages.
Persistence and eviction-risk UX:
- Call persist() on the first explicit save, except on Firefox, where it prompts. On Firefox call it only from a 'Keep my clips safe' button in My Clips settings.
- iPhone/iPad Safari tab: persist() will be false, and ITP can wipe IndexedDB and OPFS after 7 days of Safari use with no visit to the site.
  - The clip-ready sheet shows 'Save to Photos 📸' next to Share. Both open the share sheet; show a picture that points at 'Save Video'.
  - The My Clips header says 'Your clips live in Safari. Save favorites to Photos! 📸'.
  - An install nudge reuses IOSInstallPrompt through a new reason='clips' prop. It shows at most once per 14 days, respects useStartOverlayShowing, and has a first step 'Save your clips to Photos first' whenever the library is not empty, because the Home Screen app has separate storage.
  - Clips never shared and older than 3 days get a small 📸 dot.
- Home Screen web app: persist() is true and the app is exempt from ITP. No nags.
- Android or desktop Chrome: nag only when persisted is false and (free space < 1 GiB, or 10 or more clips).
- estimate.quota < 2 GiB (Chromebook guest or incognito): 'Clips might not stay on this computer. Save or share the ones you love! 📸'.
- Safari Private Browsing (OPFS throws) uses IndexedDB, or memory if that fails: 'Clips go away when you close this tab. Share or save them! 📸'.
- Optional eviction detector: a server-set HttpOnly cookie hh_clips_n (count only) through POST /api/clips/hint. HTTP-set cookies are not in ITP's JS-cookie cap. When the cookie says N > 0 but the library is empty and nothing is hosted, show once: 'Some old clips were cleaned up because we did not play for a while. Save favorites to Photos next time! 📸'.

9. REPO INTEGRATION POINTS
- apps/web/src/shared/clips/{config,ClipService,CaptureClock,FrameMeter,Governor,Compositor,lifecycle,library,recovery,store}.ts, clips-engine.worker.ts, clip-tap.worklet.ts.
- GameShell gets a ClipProvider and a header button placed after FullscreenButton (never before the title; see the adventure.css nth-child rule), plus pause-menu spokenExtras.
- auth-client.ts signOutAndClear calls ClipService.onSignOut() before clearing.
- Device keys use the 'hanks-hits-clips-*' prefix with no cleared suffix, so they survive sign-out.
- IOSInstallPrompt gets a reason prop.
- New test doubles: src/__tests__/opfs-mock.ts, src/__tests__/webcodecs-mock.ts, plus fake-indexeddb.

10. SHIP GATES
- Unit tests:
  - CaptureClock at 30/41/60/90/120/144 Hz: average 29-31 fps, strictly increasing timestamps, no burst after a 500 ms stall, resume removes the hidden gap.
  - Governor on synthetic traces.
  - Ring eviction by time and bytes, and segment split by configKey.
  - Journal truncation.
  - Owner purge.
  - Write protocol with the fakes.
- Chrome Playwright at 4x CPU throttle: fps impact <= 10%, and a produced clip decodes with duration within +/-0.2 s.
- Real devices before defaults go ON: iPhone 11 (iOS 26/27, tab and Home Screen), iPhone XR (iOS 18), iPad (26), a 4 GB Android, a 2-3 GB Android, a school Chromebook, and Windows.
  - Soak 15 min of always-on per heavy game with the Safari Web Inspector memory timeline. Pass: no jetsam, and page memory growth under 50 MB after warm-up.
  - Measure battery delta with capture on versus off.
- Crash drills: force-quit during Record, then confirm the rescue works.
risksAndMitigations: Hardware encoder cold start: the first encoder in a Chrome process gave no output for 7.5-32 s (measured on macOS; other platforms unknown). Mitigations: a site-idle 64x64 pre-warm (measured to remove the stall on later pages and tabs), a WARMING state with honest UI, a 2.5 s watchdog, a software bridge on desktop-class devices, and coldStartMs logging per device.

iPhone jetsam: the WebContent limit is about 1.5 GB, and EmulatorJS reports page-memory growth under sustained per-frame canvas work. Mitigations: iPhone heavy games run at T1 (about 33 MB incremental), the compositor is an OffscreenCanvas that is never in the DOM, replay defaults OFF for retro-arcade on iPhone, a crash-loop breaker uses an unclean-exit marker, and a 15-minute Web Inspector soak is a release gate.

Safari tab storage wipe: ITP deletes IndexedDB and OPFS after 7 days of Safari use with no visit, and persist() is never granted outside Home Screen apps. Mitigations: 'Save to Photos' is a first-class action, the My Clips shelf notice, an install nudge that says to save clips first (Home Screen storage is separate), an optional HttpOnly hint cookie to tell the kid the truth after a wipe, and hosted copies for signed-in kids through the hosting track.

The governor cannot attribute GPU or thermal load exactly. Mitigations: compare against a capture-off baseline, fall back to RESTING when stepping down does not help, never resume while fps with capture off is below 90% of baseline, and suppress stepping during clip finalization.

WebCodecs reclaims inactive codecs (10 s rule), or a GPU-process crash kills the encoder. Mitigations: proactively flush and close after 8 s idle, recreate on QuotaExceededError, and an error ladder (same config, then software, then lower tier, then disabled) capped at 4 failures in 60 s.

The avcC changes after encoder re-creation and would corrupt a clip that spans it. Mitigations: tag every GOP with a configKey hash, and assemble clips from the latest segment only. Keeping one encoder alive across short pauses makes splits rare.

Orientation or fullscreen changes mid-session would force an encoder reconfigure. Mitigation: output dims are fixed per session and the compositor letterboxes. New dims apply only on the next session.

A kid on a shared device switches accounts without a reload (credentials signIn redirect:false), and the previous kid's replay ring would leak. Mitigation: purge the rings and jobs on any session user id change and on the sign-out broadcast.

A tab crash or OS kill during a long Record. Mitigations: fMP4 fragments every 1 s go to OPFS with an fsync'd journal every 2 s and on hidden, a Web Locks ownership check, and startup recovery that truncates to the last good mdat and then remuxes.

The library fills the device or hits QuotaExceededError. Mitigations: estimate() pre-check, a 2 GiB / 25% cap, auto clips expire first, explicit clips are never auto-deleted, a shelf-full chooser, and the new clip is held in memory until the kid decides.
Records over 50 MB cannot be shared through Chromium's web share. Mitigation: Record is capped at 180 s at 1.9 Mbps video (about 45.6 MB), with a 15 s warning.

Safari Private Browsing has no OPFS, and Chromebook guest sessions are ephemeral. Mitigations: IndexedDB or memory fallback plus explicit 'clips go away' copy, using a quota < 2 GiB heuristic to warn.

A/V drift or offset from interrupted AudioContexts on iOS. Mitigations: getOutputTimestamp anchors every 2 s and on resume, zero-fill during suspended or interrupted periods, and constant 1-frame video-lead compensation.
Iframe games report rAF times against their own timeOrigin. Mitigation: convert with the timeOrigin delta in the iframe source adapter, with a unit test.
Kids tap Clip during WARMING or RESTING and get nothing. Mitigations: in RESTING, Clip still uses the retained ring. In WARMING, a spoken toast explains the wait. Neither state ever fails silently.
Firefox persist() shows a permission prompt a kid cannot judge. Mitigation: call it only from an explicit grown-up-facing button in My Clips settings.
rejectedAlternatives: IndexedDB-only Blob storage for clips. It needs the whole MP4 in RAM before put() (about 2x size spike), cannot do positioned streaming writes for fast-start muxing, and gets the same ITP and quota eviction as OPFS. It stays only as a fallback for Private Browsing or OPFS failure, with clips <= 30 s.
Cache API for clip bytes. It has the same eviction, no random-access writes, and the wrong abstraction.
Relying on navigator.storage.persist() in Safari tabs. WebKit grants it only to app-bound, managed or standalone Home Screen domains (NetworkStorageManager::persistOrigin).
Holding raw VideoFrames in the ring. That is about 1.4 MB per 720p NV12 frame, or about 2.5 GB for 60 s: an instant jetsam.
A MediaRecorder rolling ring. Chunks after the first are not independently decodable. MediaRecorder stays only as the T0 manual-Record fallback.

Encoding audio continuously with native AudioEncoder into the ring. iOS < 26 has no AudioEncoder, and the WebKit AAC decoder-config bug (302253) is only fixed inside mediabunny's own wrapper. Keep an Int16 PCM ring and let mediabunny encode at clip time.
A Float32 PCM ring. It doubles audio memory (23 MB per 60 s) for no audible gain.

Synthetic constant-frame-rate timestamps (frameIndex x 33.3 ms). They judder at 144 Hz or 41 fps sources and speed video up after game stalls. Use real rAF-based VFR timestamps with slot pacing instead.
performance.now() inside the callback as the frame timestamp. It jitters by the work done in earlier callbacks, whereas the rAF timestamp is vsync-aligned.
Reconfiguring the encoder on rotation or fullscreen. The segment splits would silently shorten clips. Letterbox into fixed per-session dims instead.

A DOM-attached compositor canvas for the WebCodecs path. It adds a composited layer, which is risky on iOS given the EmulatorJS page-memory report. It is kept only for captureStream, which WebKit needs attached.
Periodic capture-off A/B probes during buffering to measure the baseline. They punch holes in the replay. Use persisted baselines, the first 2 s of play, and refresh from RESTING periods instead.
Deleting a kid's clips on sign-out to protect the next kid. That loses clips. Hide them by owner partition instead, and offer an explicit grown-up removal option.
Battery Status API or navigator.deviceMemory as the primary device signal. Both are Chrome-only. Use observed frame pacing, calibration, UA Version floors, and learned per-device history instead.
Always-on replay by default on every device. It is unsafe on T0, and on T1 heavy games on iPhone. Use a decision table plus the crash breaker.
A disk-backed OPFS ring to save RAM. It would save only about 20 MB on iPhone T1 at the cost of continuous flash writes and complexity. It is not worth it given the measured budgets.
openQuestions: The encoder cold-start stall (7.5-32 s) was measured only on Chrome 153 on macOS. Does it happen on Android Chrome (MediaCodec), ChromeOS and iOS Safari (VideoToolbox), and does the idle pre-warm fix it there too?

On a real iPhone, does drawImage or createImageBitmap from a preserveDrawingBuffer:false WebGL canvas in the same task give non-blank frames? And does sustained OffscreenCanvas compositing grow Safari 'page' memory the way EmulatorJS #1220 describes? Both need the soak gate.
Does Safari (iOS 26/27) give same-origin iframe rAF timestamps relative to the iframe's timeOrigin, as the spec implies? A small device test settles it.
Is @mediabunny/aac-encoder (libavcodec-based WASM) acceptable on license and bundle size as the Safari < 26 AAC fallback, and do iOS Photos accept its output?

Should the optional server pieces ship: the HttpOnly eviction-hint cookie endpoint and a values-free diagnostics beacon (tier, level changes, unclean exits)? They make tuning and honest eviction messaging possible, but they add server surface.

Chrome Android: do hardware H.264 encoders on low-end MediaTek/Unisoc devices accept 1024x576 and 848x480 at level 3.1 in realtime mode, or do some need Baseline only? The calibration handles it, but device data would set better defaults.

iOS Low Power Mode inference relies on a stored max Hz. Is a first-ever session in LPM (no history) acceptable at T1 defaults, or should LPM be treated as eco whenever steady 30 Hz is seen on an iPhone?
Retro-arcade on iPhone may already jetsam without any recording (EmulatorJS #1220). Should that pre-existing instability be verified and filed separately from this feature?

verdicts.claim: MEASURED: the first hardware H.264 VideoEncoder in a Chrome process takes 7.5-32 s to emit output; a 64x64 idle pre-warm removes the stall for later encoders; prefer-software has no stall.
verdicts.correction: The stall is real, but it is not specific to fresh profiles or Playwright. I reproduced it with Chrome 153.0.8010.53 on macOS 26.5.1 (M5), launched directly with no Playwright flags: 10.5-17.0 s. It comes back on EVERY browser-process launch, even with a reused profile, and 30 s of idle before the first configure did not shorten it (13.7 s). It is not VideoToolbox itself: ffmpeg h264_videotoolbox does its first encode in 0.28-0.43 s including process start. The pre-warm helps only if it starts 10-17 s before the game's encoder is needed, so a kid who taps a game within ~15 s of opening Chrome still waits. The software bridge works: a prefer-software 1280x720 encoder created 2.5 s into a pending hardware warm-up produced output ~90 ms later and encoded 90/90 frames, while the hardware warm-up finished at 10.6-12.7 s. Later hardware encoders then give first output in 23-24 ms.
sources: ffmpeg -c:v h264_videotoolbox timing run in this session (0.28-0.43 s)

verdicts.claim: MEASURED per-frame capture cost (p95 0.2 ms at 1x, 1.0-1.9 ms at 4-6x) for drawImage into a compositor, then new VideoFrame, then transfer; OffscreenCanvas and createImageBitmap variants cost the same.
verdicts.correction: These are Chrome-desktop numbers and do not carry over to WebKit (every iOS browser). In WebKit main, new VideoFrame(OffscreenCanvas) and new VideoFrame(ImageBitmap) both go through WebCodecsVideoFrame::create(ImageBuffer&), which does a synchronous imageBuffer.getPixelBuffer (unpremultiplied BGRA8 readback) and then VideoFrame::createFromPixelBuffer (another copy). new VideoFrame(HTMLCanvasElement) with a 2D context takes the same readback path; the source carries a FIXME saying it should be optimized. Only an HTMLCanvasElement with a WebGL context gets a GPU-side IOSurface copy (surfaceBufferToVideoFrame, then copySurfaceBuffer, then CVPixelBuffer). So on iPhone, the spec's path is a per-frame synchronous readback of 1.6-2.4 MB (T1/T2), and with the GPU process it is also a sync IPC. That cost has not been measured.
sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WebKit/WebKit/main/Source/WebCore/html/HTMLCanvasElement.cpp (toVideoFrame lines 831-862, FIXME 'specializing toVideoFrame() ... to not use getPixelBuffer()')

verdicts.claim: persist() succeeds only for app-bound, managed, or standalone (Home Screen) domains, so it is effectively always false in a Safari tab; the default time-based eviction interval is 7*24h.
verdicts.correction: persistOrigin grants when the domain is in registrableDomainsExemptFromWebsiteDataDeletion. That set is appBound, managed, m_persistedDomains and standalone. The track left out m_persistedDomains.
